Duluth has historically been a hub for industry with limited availability of vacant land for large-scale solar within city limits. Incorporating solar onto existing assets reduces the City’s operating costs, carbon footprint, greenhouse gas emissions, and personnel time. Additionally, utilizing infrastructure with solar as a secondary use saves larger swaths of land for partnership with private entities that help to drive business and industrial investment in the community. Developing an array on existing site also allows the City to use cost savings by covering the pumping station electrical load that resides on that site. The pumping station uses approximately 225,000 kWh a year, costing the City an average of $38,625 a year. With net metering allowing up to 120% of the load on any particular site in Minnesota Power territory, the City of Duluth could save a maximum of approximately $46,000 a year. That means over the projected 25-year life-span of the proposed project, the City could save $1.15 Million in operating costs- funding that can be reinvested to encourage additional renewable energy development. Through input from the CIT and expanded conversations with Minnesota Power due to the RACER project, the City and Minnesota Power began exploring how the remaining approximate 1,000,000 kWh per year of estimated annual average generation on site in excess of the allowed 120% of energy consumption under net metering provisions, could be used offset low-moderate income household energy costs addressing energy burdens and building greater economic resilience. This potential partnership with Minnesota Power would allow for flexibility to use the extra energy generation on City land to benefit community members in ways that other municipalities might not be able to. Putting the extra approximate 1,000,000 kWh hours generated into community solar would save approximately 200 detached single-family households, each receiving the benefit of 4kW of the array, an average of $669 per year. In addition to the benefit provided to the Duluth economy and reduction of household energy burdens, the Bayview project would benefit the regional economy as well. Initially envisioned under Build America Buy America requirements, the proposed project and financial calculations included solar panels manufactured in Mountain Iron, Minnesota. Located just over an hour north of Duluth, this solar panel manufacturer provides over 130 local jobs on the Minnesota Iron Range and is one of the larger employers in the Mountain Iron area.
